claims.text: A modest phosphorus increase coupled with a compensatory decrease in one transition metal will simultaneously improve glass-forming ability and amorphous-state thermal stability.
The baseline phosphorus-containing alloy typically has limited glass formation and moderate thermal stability.
Cooling rates of approximately 10^4–10^6 K/s are conventional for the proposed melt-spinning or suction-casting conditions.
The beneficial effect requires a narrow composition window that avoids phase separation.
Optimizing atomic-size distribution and mixing enthalpy can improve atomic packing in the amorphous alloy.
Improved atomic packing favors greater local disorder and stabilizes the amorphous energy landscape.
The added phosphorus acts as a network former and increases atomic connectivity.
Increased network connectivity raises the nucleation barrier for crystallization.
The phosphorus adjustment increases configurational entropy.
Greater configurational entropy can affect atomic packing and contribute to resistance against crystallization in high-entropy metallic glasses.
The modified alloy will have a larger critical casting diameter or a higher amorphous fraction than the baseline.
The modified alloy will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than the baseline.
Critical casting diameter is a measure of glass-forming ability in high-entropy bulk metallic glasses.
If phosphorus is already near saturation or induces phase separation, further phosphorus addition may provide no benefit or may destabilize the amorphous structure.
Small element substitutions or additions can adjust atomic-size-related lattice distortion and thereby influence phase selection in high-entropy alloys.
